idiom_name: Spring Integration claim-check transformers plus an inline value class for the token
implementation_notes: Kotlin inherits the JVM machinery unchanged: Spring Integration's claim-check-in stores the payload in a MessageStore and replaces it with a generated id, and claim-check-out redeems (and optionally removes) it, so there is no Kotlin-specific structure to write. Kotlin contributes at the edges - an @JvmInline value class turns the raw id into a ClaimCheckId so the token cannot be mixed up with any other string, and withContext(Dispatchers.IO) keeps store I/O off the dispatcher that carries messages, which matters because the transformers block. Hand-rolled stores (a JMS text message plus a JDBC row or an object-store key) remain the fallback for non-Spring services, where the claim-once and retention rules must be reimplemented carefully.
pitfalls: Value-class tokens are erased: two different @JvmInline wrappers over String are the same type to Java, reflection and most serializers, so a ClaimCheckId can be smuggled where an ordinary id is expected.
Store I/O must not run on the same dispatcher that consumes messages - a blocking JDBC fetch inside a coroutine stalls the consumer exactly like a blocking call in Java would.

Cancellation does not roll back a claim: a claim-check-out cancelled after restoring the payload but before remove-message leaves the payload stored or half-consumed, which is worse than a clean failure.
